formulas: Company: artificial person created by law, separate legal entity
Features: separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability, transferability of shares
Types: Private Company, Public Company, One Person Company (OPC)
Private Company: min 2, max 200 members; min 2 directors
Public Company: min 7 members, no max; min 3 directors
OPC: only 1 member, 1 director
Share Capital: money raised by issue of shares
Authorised Capital: max capital a company can raise
Issued Capital: part of authorised capital offered for subscription
Subscribed Capital: part of issued capital subscribed by public
Called-up Capital: part of subscribed capital called by company
Paid-up Capital: part of called-up capital actually paid
Reserve Capital: part of uncalled capital reserved
Equity Shares: ordinary shares, voting rights, variable dividend
Preference Shares: preferential dividend, no voting rights
Types of Preference Shares: Cumulative, Non-cumulative, Participating, Non-participating, Convertible, Non-convertible, Redeemable, Irredeemable
Debentures: borrowed capital, fixed interest, no voting rights
derivations: Explain the features of a company.

Proof: Features: (1) Separate legal entity: company is distinct from its members. (2) Perpetual succession: company continues even if members change. (3) Limited liability: liability of members limited to unpaid amount on shares. (4) Transferability of shares: shares can be transferred. (5) Common seal: official signature of company. (6) Artificial person: created by law. (7) Separate property: company owns property in its own name. (8) Capacity to sue and be sued.
Explain the difference between Private Company and Public Company.

Proof: (1) Private: min 2, max 200 members; Public: min 7, no max. (2) Private: min 2 directors; Public: min 3 directors. (3) Private: shares not freely transferable; Public: shares freely transferable. (4) Private: can start business after incorporation; Public: needs certificate of commencement. (5) Private: no need to issue prospectus; Public: must issue prospectus. (6) Private: 'Pvt. Ltd.' suffix; Public: 'Ltd.' suffix.
Explain the types of share capital.

Proof: (1) Authorised/Nominal/Registered Capital: max capital a company can raise. (2) Issued Capital: part of authorised capital offered for subscription. (3) Subscribed Capital: part of issued capital subscribed by public. (4) Called-up Capital: part of subscribed capital called by company. (5) Paid-up Capital: part of called-up capital actually paid. (6) Reserve Capital: part of uncalled capital reserved for winding up.
Explain the difference between Equity Shares and Preference Shares.

Proof: (1) Equity: ordinary shares; Preference: preferential shares. (2) Equity: dividend after preference; Preference: fixed/preferential dividend. (3) Equity: voting rights; Preference: no voting rights (except in some cases). (4) Equity: refund after preference; Preference: refund before equity. (5) Equity: variable dividend; Preference: fixed dividend. (6) Equity: higher risk; Preference: lower risk.
Explain the difference between Shares and Debentures.

Proof: (1) Shares: ownership capital; Debentures: borrowed capital. (2) Shares: dividend; Debentures: interest. (3) Shares: no fixed rate; Debentures: fixed rate. (4) Shares: voting rights; Debentures: no voting rights. (5) Shares: refund after debentures; Debentures: refund before shares. (6) Shares: not secured; Debentures: may be secured. (7) Shares: not convertible; Debentures: convertible.
Explain the types of Preference Shares.

Proof: (1) Cumulative: unpaid dividend accumulates. (2) Non-cumulative: unpaid dividend does not accumulate. (3) Participating: share in surplus profits. (4) Non-participating: no share in surplus profits. (5) Convertible: can be converted into equity shares. (6) Non-convertible: cannot be converted. (7) Redeemable: can be redeemed after a period. (8) Irredeemable: cannot be redeemed (now not allowed in India).

derivations: Explain the accounting treatment for issue of shares at par.

Proof: Steps: (1) On application: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Application A/c. (2) On allotment: Share Application A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c. (3) On allotment money due: Share Allotment A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c. (4) On receipt of allotment money: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Allotment A/c. (5) Similarly for calls.
Explain the accounting treatment for issue of shares at premium.

Proof: Premium amount is credited to Securities Premium A/c. Entry: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c To Securities Premium A/c. Securities Premium can be used for: (1) Issue of bonus shares. (2) Writing off preliminary expenses. (3) Writing off discount on issue of shares/debentures. (4) Buy-back of shares.
Explain the accounting treatment for calls in arrears.

Proof: Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. To Share Allotment/Call A/c. Interest on Calls in Arrears: Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. To Interest on Calls in Arrears A/c. If shares are forfeited, calls in arrears is transferred to Share Forfeiture A/c.
Explain the accounting treatment for calls in advance.
Proof: Bank A/c Dr. To Calls in Advance A/c. Interest on Calls in Advance: Interest on Calls in Advance A/c Dr. To Bank A/c. Calls in Advance is shown as a liability in Balance Sheet.
Explain the accounting treatment for forfeiture of shares.

Proof: Share Capital A/c Dr. (Called-up amount) To Share Forfeiture A/c (Amount received) To Calls in Arrears A/c (Amount not received). If shares were issued at premium and premium not received, Securities Premium A/c is also debited.
Explain the accounting treatment for re-issue of forfeited shares.

Proof: Bank A/c Dr. (Re-issue price) Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. (Discount on re-issue) To Share Capital A/c (Paid-up amount). If re-issued at premium, Securities Premium A/c is credited. Balance in Share Forfeiture A/c is transferred to Capital Reserve A/c.

Share and Share Capital.notes: Chapter 10: Share and Share Capital. Key points: (1) Share: unit of ownership. (2) Share Capital types: Authorised, Issued, Subscribed, Called-up, Paid-up, Reserve. (3) Issue at par, premium, discount. (4) Calls in Arrears: amount not paid. (5) Calls in Advance: amount paid early. (6) Interest on Calls in Arrears and Advance. (7) Forfeiture of shares for non-payment. (8) Re-issue of forfeited shares. (9) Securities Premium uses. (10) Capital Reserve from forfeiture.

formulas: Issue of Shares: raising capital by issuing shares
At Par: issue price = face value
At Premium: issue price > face value
At Discount: issue price < face value (now not allowed)
Application Money: paid at time of applying
Allotment Money: paid at time of allotment
Call Money: paid when called by company
Calls in Arrears: amount not paid by shareholders
Calls in Advance: amount paid before due date
Interest on Calls in Arrears: charged by company @ 10% p.a.
Interest on Calls in Advance: paid by company @ 12% p.a.
Share Forfeiture: cancellation of shares for non-payment
Re-issue of Forfeited Shares: at par, premium, or discount
Securities Premium: amount received above face value
Capital Reserve: balance in Share Forfeiture A/c after re-issue
Pro-rata Allotment: allotment in proportion to application
derivations: Explain the accounting treatment for issue of shares at par.

Proof: Steps: (1) On application: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Application A/c. (2) On allotment: Share Application A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c. (3) On allotment money due: Share Allotment A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c. (4) On receipt of allotment money: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Allotment A/c. (5) Similarly for calls.
Explain the accounting treatment for issue of shares at premium.

Proof: Premium amount is credited to Securities Premium A/c. Entry: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c To Securities Premium A/c. Securities Premium can be used for: (1) Issue of bonus shares. (2) Writing off preliminary expenses. (3) Writing off discount on issue of shares/debentures. (4) Buy-back of shares.
Explain the accounting treatment for pro-rata allotment.

Proof: When applications are more than shares offered, allotment is made in proportion. Excess application money is adjusted towards allotment. Entry: Share Application A/c Dr. To Share Allotment A/c (excess adjusted) To Share Capital A/c (actual allotment).
Explain the accounting treatment for calls in arrears.

Proof: Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. To Share Allotment/Call A/c. Interest on Calls in Arrears: Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. To Interest on Calls in Arrears A/c. If shares are forfeited, calls in arrears is transferred to Share Forfeiture A/c.
Explain the accounting treatment for calls in advance.
Proof: Bank A/c Dr. To Calls in Advance A/c. Interest on Calls in Advance: Interest on Calls in Advance A/c Dr. To Bank A/c. Calls in Advance is shown as a liability in Balance Sheet.
Explain the accounting treatment for forfeiture and re-issue of shares.

Proof: Forfeiture: Share Capital A/c Dr. To Share Forfeiture A/c To Calls in Arrears A/c. Re-issue: Bank A/c Dr. Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c. Balance in Share Forfeiture A/c transferred to Capital Reserve A/c.

formulas: Forfeiture: cancellation of shares due to non-payment of calls
Share Forfeiture A/c: records amount received on forfeited shares
Forfeiture entry: Share Capital A/c Dr. To Share Forfeiture A/c To Calls in Arrears A/c
If shares issued at premium and premium not received: Securities Premium A/c also debited
If shares issued at premium and premium already received: Securities Premium not debited
Re-issue: forfeited shares issued again
Re-issue at par: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c
Re-issue at discount: Bank A/c Dr. Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c
Re-issue at premium: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c To Securities Premium A/c
Capital Reserve = Share Forfeiture (on forfeited shares) - Discount on re-issue
Balance in Share Forfeiture A/c after re-issue transferred to Capital Reserve
If only part of forfeited shares re-issued, proportionate amount transferred
Calls in Arrears: amount not paid by shareholder
Calls in Advance: amount paid before due date
Pro-rata allotment: excess application money adjusted
derivations: Explain the accounting treatment for forfeiture of shares.

Proof: Forfeiture entry: Share Capital A/c Dr. (Called-up amount) To Share Forfeiture A/c (Amount received) To Calls in Arrears A/c (Amount not received). If shares were issued at premium and premium not received, Securities Premium A/c is also debited. If premium already received, Securities Premium is not debited.
Explain the accounting treatment for re-issue of forfeited shares.

Proof: Re-issue at par: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c. Re-issue at discount: Bank A/c Dr. Share Forfeiture A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c. Re-issue at premium: Bank A/c Dr. To Share Capital A/c To Securities Premium A/c. Balance in Share Forfeiture A/c after re-issue transferred to Capital Reserve A/c.
How to calculate Capital Reserve on re-issue?

Proof: Capital Reserve = Share Forfeiture (on forfeited shares) - Discount on re-issue. If re-issued at premium, no discount, so full Share Forfeiture transferred to Capital Reserve. If only part re-issued, proportionate amount transferred.
Explain the treatment of calls in arrears on forfeiture.
Proof: Calls in Arrears A/c is credited on forfeiture. If calls in arrears is already recorded, it is transferred to Share Forfeiture A/c. Entry: Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. To Share Forfeiture A/c.
Explain the treatment of Securities Premium on forfeiture.

Proof: If shares issued at premium and premium not received, Securities Premium A/c is debited along with Share Capital A/c. If premium already received, Securities Premium is not debited. Entry: Share Capital A/c Dr. Securities Premium A/c Dr. To Share Forfeiture A/c To Calls in Arrears A/c.
Explain pro-rata allotment and its treatment.

Proof: When applications are more than shares offered, allotment is made in proportion. Excess application money is adjusted towards allotment. Entry: Share Application A/c Dr. To Share Allotment A/c (excess adjusted) To Share Capital A/c (actual allotment).

formulas: Balance Sheet: statement of assets and liabilities
Share Capital: shown under Shareholders' Funds
Authorised Capital: shown in notes to accounts
Issued Capital: shown in notes to accounts
Subscribed Capital: shown in notes to accounts
Called-up Capital: shown in notes to accounts
Paid-up Capital: shown in notes to accounts
Equity Share Capital: shown separately
Preference Share Capital: shown separately

Calls in Advance: shown as liability
Share Forfeiture A/c: shown as addition to Share Capital
Securities Premium: shown under Reserves and Surplus
Capital Reserve: shown under Reserves and Surplus
Format: Equity and Liabilities + Assets
Shareholders' Funds = Share Capital + Reserves and Surplus
Non-Current Liabilities = Long-term borrowings, Deferred tax, Long-term provisions
Current Liabilities = Short-term borrowings, Trade payables, Short-term provisions
Non-Current Assets = Fixed assets, Non-current investments, Long-term loans
Current Assets = Current investments, Inventories, Trade receivables, Cash and cash equivalents
derivations: Explain the format of Company's Balance Sheet.

Proof: As per Schedule III of Companies Act 2013: Equity and Liabilities: (1) Shareholders' Funds: Share Capital, Reserves and Surplus, Money received against share warrants. (2) Share Application Money Pending Allotment. (3) Non-Current Liabilities: Long-term borrowings, Deferred tax liabilities, Other long-term liabilities, Long-term provisions. (4) Current Liabilities: Short-term borrowings, Trade payables, Other current liabilities, Short-term provisions. Assets: (1) Non-Current Assets: Fixed assets, Non-current investments, Deferred tax assets, Long-term loans and advances, Other non-current assets. (2) Current Assets: Current investments, Inventories, Trade receivables, Cash and cash equivalents, Short-term loans and advances, Other current assets.
Explain the disclosure of Share Capital in Balance Sheet.

Proof: Share Capital is shown under Shareholders' Funds. In notes to accounts: (1) Authorised Capital: number of shares and amount. (2) Issued Capital: number of shares and amount. (3) Subscribed Capital: number of shares and amount. (4) Called-up Capital: number of shares and amount. (5) Paid-up Capital: number of shares and amount. (6) Calls in Arrears: deducted. (7) Calls in Advance: shown as liability. (8) Share Forfeiture A/c: added to Share Capital.
Explain the treatment of Calls in Arrears in Balance Sheet.

Proof: Calls in Arrears is deducted from Subscribed Capital but added back to Called-up Capital. In notes: Subscribed Capital: X. Less: Calls in Arrears: Y. Called-up Capital: X-Y. Add: Calls in Advance: Z. Paid-up Capital: X-Y+Z.
Explain the treatment of Share Forfeiture A/c in Balance Sheet.
Proof: Share Forfeiture A/c is shown as an addition to Share Capital in the Balance Sheet. It is not shown as a separate item. In notes: Share Capital: X. Add: Share Forfeiture A/c: Y. Total: X+Y.
Explain the treatment of Securities Premium in Balance Sheet.
Proof: Securities Premium is shown under Reserves and Surplus. It is a capital reserve and is not available for distribution as dividend. It can be used for specific purposes as per Companies Act.
Explain the difference between Authorised, Issued, Subscribed, Called-up and Paid-up Capital.

Proof: (1) Authorised: max capital a company can raise. (2) Issued: part of authorised offered for subscription. (3) Subscribed: part of issued subscribed by public. (4) Called-up: part of subscribed called by company. (5) Paid-up: part of called-up actually paid.

formulas: Debenture: borrowed capital, fixed interest, no voting rights
Issue of Debentures: at par, at premium, at discount
At Par: issue price = face value
At Premium: issue price > face value
At Discount: issue price < face value
Debenture Interest: fixed rate, paid periodically
Interest on Debentures: charged to P&L A/c
Tax Deducted at Source (TDS): deducted on interest
Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR): created for redemption
Debenture Redemption Investment (DRI): invested for redemption
Issue of Debentures as Collateral Security: for bank loan
Debentures issued for consideration other than cash: to vendors
Journal entry for issue at par: Bank A/c Dr. To Debentures A/c
Journal entry for issue at premium: Bank A/c Dr. To Debentures A/c To Securities Premium A/c
Journal entry for issue at discount: Bank A/c Dr. Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c Dr. To Debentures A/c
Interest entry: Debenture Interest A/c Dr. To Bank A/c To TDS Payable A/c

Proof: Entry: Bank A/c Dr. To Debentures A/c. Interest: Debenture Interest A/c Dr. To Bank A/c. TDS: Debenture Interest A/c Dr. To Bank A/c To TDS Payable A/c. Debenture Interest transferred to P&L A/c.

formulas: Redemption: repayment of debentures to debenture holders
Methods: (1) Lump sum payment, (2) Installment payment, (3) Purchase in open market, (4) Conversion into shares
Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR): created for redemption
DRR = 25% of nominal value of debentures (as per Companies Act 2013)
Debenture Redemption Investment (DRI): invested for redemption
DRI = 15% of nominal value of debentures
DRR and DRI mandatory for listed companies and NBFCs
For unlisted companies, DRR = 25% of debentures
Redemption entry: Debentures A/c Dr. To Debenture Holders A/c
Payment entry: Debenture Holders A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
DRR entry: Surplus A/c Dr. To DRR A/c
DRI entry: DRI A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
On redemption: DRR A/c Dr. To General Reserve A/c
DRI encashed: Bank A/c Dr. To DRI A/c
Interest on DRI: DRI A/c Dr. To Interest on DRI A/c
Purchase in open market: Debentures A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
If purchase price < face value: profit credited to P&L A/c
If purchase price > face value: loss debited to P&L A/c
Conversion: Debentures A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c To Securities Premium A/c
derivations: Explain the methods of redemption of debentures.

Proof: Methods: (1) Lump sum payment: entire amount paid at maturity. (2) Installment payment: paid in installments over period. (3) Purchase in open market: company buys its own debentures from market. (4) Conversion into shares: debentures converted into equity shares. (5) Sinking fund method: fund created for redemption.
Explain the concept of Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR).

Proof: DRR is created out of profits to provide funds for redemption. As per Companies Act 2013, DRR = 25% of nominal value of debentures. Entry: Surplus A/c Dr. To DRR A/c. On redemption, DRR is transferred to General Reserve. DRR is mandatory for listed companies and NBFCs.
Explain the concept of Debenture Redemption Investment (DRI).

Proof: DRI is investment made for redemption. As per Companies Act 2013, DRI = 15% of nominal value of debentures. Entry: DRI A/c Dr. To Bank A/c. On redemption, DRI is encashed. Interest on DRI is credited to P&L A/c.
Explain the accounting treatment for redemption by purchase in open market.

Proof: Entry: Debentures A/c Dr. To Bank A/c (if purchase price = face value). If purchase price < face value: Debentures A/c Dr. To Bank A/c To Profit on Redemption A/c. If purchase price > face value: Debentures A/c Dr. Loss on Redemption A/c Dr. To Bank A/c.
Explain the accounting treatment for redemption by conversion into shares.

Proof: Entry: Debentures A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c To Securities Premium A/c. If converted at par: Debentures A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c. If converted at premium: Debentures A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c To Securities Premium A/c.
Explain the difference between DRR and DRI.

Proof: DRR is a reserve created out of profits, DRI is an investment made for redemption. DRR = 25% of nominal value, DRI = 15% of nominal value. DRR is transferred to General Reserve on redemption, DRI is encashed. Both are mandatory for listed companies and NBFCs.

formulas: Financial Statements: Balance Sheet, Profit and Loss Account, Cash Flow Statement
Balance Sheet: statement of assets and liabilities
Profit and Loss Account: statement of profit or loss
Schedule III: format prescribed by Companies Act 2013
Equity and Liabilities: Shareholders' Funds, Non-Current Liabilities, Current Liabilities
Assets: Non-Current Assets, Current Assets
Shareholders' Funds = Share Capital + Reserves and Surplus
Non-Current Liabilities = Long-term borrowings + Deferred tax + Long-term provisions
Current Liabilities = Short-term borrowings + Trade payables + Short-term provisions
Non-Current Assets = Fixed assets + Non-current investments + Long-term loans
Current Assets = Current investments + Inventories + Trade receivables + Cash
Revenue = Sales + Other Income
Expenses = Cost of materials + Employee benefits + Finance costs + Depreciation + Other expenses
Profit Before Tax = Revenue - Expenses
Tax = 30% of Profit Before Tax (assumed)
Profit After Tax = Profit Before Tax - Tax
Earnings Per Share (EPS) = Profit After Tax / Number of Equity Shares

formulas: Financial Analysis: process of analysing financial statements

Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
Quick Ratio = (Current Assets - Stock - Prepaid) / Current Liabilities
Debt-Equity Ratio = Debt / Equity
Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT / Interest

Debtors Turnover = Credit Sales / Average Debtors
Creditors Turnover = Credit Purchases / Average Creditors

Net Profit Ratio = Net Profit / Revenue × 100

Return on Investment = Net Profit / Capital Employed × 100

How to calculate Current Ratio and Quick Ratio?
Proof: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities. Quick Ratio = (Current Assets - Stock - Prepaid) / Current Liabilities. Ideal Current Ratio = 2:1, Ideal Quick Ratio = 1:1.
How to calculate Debt-Equity Ratio and Interest Coverage Ratio?

Proof: Debt-Equity Ratio = Debt / Equity. Debt = Long-term borrowings. Equity = Shareholders' Funds. Ideal = 2:1. Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT / Interest. EBIT = Earnings Before Interest and Tax. Higher ratio means better ability to pay interest.
How to calculate Gross Profit Ratio, Net Profit Ratio, and Operating Ratio?

Proof: Gross Profit Ratio = Gross Profit / Revenue × 100. Net Profit Ratio = Net Profit / Revenue × 100. Operating Ratio = Operating Cost / Revenue × 100. Operating Cost = Cost of Goods Sold + Operating Expenses. These ratios measure profitability.

Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold / Average Inventory
Debtors Turnover = Credit Sales / Average Debtors
Creditors Turnover = Credit Purchases / Average Creditors
Profitability Ratios: Gross Profit Ratio, Net Profit Ratio, Operating Ratio, ROI
Gross Profit Ratio = Gross Profit / Revenue × 100
Net Profit Ratio = Net Profit / Revenue × 100
Operating Ratio = Operating Cost / Revenue × 100
Return on Investment = Net Profit / Capital Employed × 100
Operating Cost = Cost of Goods Sold + Operating Expenses
Average Inventory = (Opening + Closing)/2
Average Debtors = (Opening + Closing)/2
Average Creditors = (Opening + Closing)/2
derivations: Explain Liquidity Ratios.

Proof: Liquidity Ratios measure ability to meet short-term obligations. (1) Current Ratio = Current Assets/Current Liabilities. Ideal 2:1. (2) Quick Ratio = (Current Assets - Stock - Prepaid)/Current Liabilities. Ideal 1:1. Higher ratio means better liquidity.
Explain Solvency Ratios.

Proof: Solvency Ratios measure ability to meet long-term obligations. (1) Debt-Equity Ratio = Debt/Equity. Ideal 2:1. (2) Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT/Interest. Higher ratio means better ability to pay interest.
Explain Activity Ratios.

Proof: Activity Ratios measure efficiency of asset utilisation. (1) Inventory Turnover = COGS/Average Inventory. (2) Debtors Turnover = Credit Sales/Average Debtors. (3) Creditors Turnover = Credit Purchases/Average Creditors. Higher turnover means better efficiency.
Explain Profitability Ratios.

Proof: Profitability Ratios measure earning capacity. (1) Gross Profit Ratio = GP/Revenue × 100. (2) Net Profit Ratio = NP/Revenue × 100. (3) Operating Ratio = Operating Cost/Revenue × 100. (4) ROI = NP/Capital Employed × 100. Higher ratio means better profitability.
How to calculate Current Ratio and Quick Ratio?
Proof: Current Ratio = Current Assets/Current Liabilities. Quick Ratio = (Current Assets - Stock - Prepaid)/Current Liabilities. Ideal Current Ratio = 2:1, Ideal Quick Ratio = 1:1.
How to calculate Gross Profit Ratio and Net Profit Ratio?
Proof: Gross Profit Ratio = Gross Profit/Revenue × 100. Net Profit Ratio = Net Profit/Revenue × 100. GP = Revenue - COGS. NP = GP - Operating Expenses - Interest - Tax.

formulas: Cash Flow Statement: shows inflow and outflow of cash
Categories: Operating Activities, Investing Activities, Financing Activities
Operating Activities: main revenue-generating activities
Investing Activities: purchase/sale of fixed assets, investments
Financing Activities: issue of shares, borrowings, repayment
Cash from Operating = Net Profit + Non-Cash Expenses - Non-Cash Income ± Changes in Working Capital
Cash from Investing = Sale of Assets - Purchase of Assets - Purchase of Investments + Sale of Investments
Cash from Financing = Issue of Shares + Borrowings - Repayment - Interest Paid - Dividend Paid
Net Increase/Decrease = Operating + Investing + Financing
Opening Cash + Net Increase = Closing Cash
Non-Cash Expenses: Depreciation, Amortisation, Provisions
Non-Cash Income: Profit on Sale of Assets
Working Capital Changes: Current Assets and Current Liabilities
derivations: Explain the Cash Flow Statement.

Proof: Cash Flow Statement shows inflow and outflow of cash during a period. It has three categories: (1) Operating Activities: main revenue-generating activities. (2) Investing Activities: purchase/sale of fixed assets, investments. (3) Financing Activities: issue of shares, borrowings, repayment. It reconciles opening and closing cash balances.
Explain Operating Activities.

Proof: Operating Activities are the main revenue-generating activities. Cash from Operating = Net Profit + Non-Cash Expenses - Non-Cash Income ± Changes in Working Capital. Non-Cash Expenses: Depreciation, Amortisation. Non-Cash Income: Profit on Sale of Assets. Working Capital Changes: Current Assets and Current Liabilities.
Explain Investing Activities.

Proof: Investing Activities include purchase and sale of fixed assets and investments. Cash from Investing = Sale of Assets - Purchase of Assets - Purchase of Investments + Sale of Investments. These activities affect long-term assets.
Explain Financing Activities.

Proof: Financing Activities include issue of shares, borrowings, repayment, interest paid, dividend paid. Cash from Financing = Issue of Shares + Borrowings - Repayment - Interest Paid - Dividend Paid. These activities affect capital and borrowings.
How to prepare Cash Flow Statement?

Proof: Steps: (1) Calculate cash from operating activities. (2) Calculate cash from investing activities. (3) Calculate cash from financing activities. (4) Net increase/decrease = Operating + Investing + Financing. (5) Opening Cash + Net Increase = Closing Cash.
Explain the difference between Cash Flow Statement and Balance Sheet.

Proof: Cash Flow Statement shows inflow and outflow of cash over a period. Balance Sheet shows financial position at a point of time. Cash Flow Statement is dynamic, Balance Sheet is static. Cash Flow Statement is prepared for a period, Balance Sheet is prepared on a date.

formulas: GDP (Gross Domestic Product): market value of all final goods and services produced within domestic territory
GNP (Gross National Product) = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)
NNP (Net National Product) = GNP - Depreciation
NNP at Factor Cost = NNP at Market Price - Indirect Taxes + Subsidies
National Income = NNP at Factor Cost
GDP at Market Price = GDP at Factor Cost + Indirect Taxes - Subsidies
Personal Income = National Income - Corporate Tax - Retained Earnings + Transfer Payments
Disposable Income = Personal Income - Direct Taxes
Private Income = Personal Income + Corporate Tax + Retained Earnings
Value Added = Output - Intermediate Consumption
Expenditure Method: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)
Income Method: GDP = Compensation of Employees + Operating Surplus + Mixed Income + Consumption of Fixed Capital
Product Method: GDP = Σ Value Added by all firms
Real GDP = Nominal GDP / Price Index × 100
GDP Deflator = Nominal GDP / Real GDP × 100
derivations: Explain the three methods of measuring National Income.

Proof: (1) Product Method: Sum of value added by all firms = GDP. Value Added = Output - Intermediate Consumption. (2) Income Method: GDP = Compensation of Employees + Operating Surplus + Mixed Income + Consumption of Fixed Capital. (3) Expenditure Method: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M). All three methods give same GDP.
Explain the relationship between GDP, GNP, NNP, and National Income.

Proof: GDP = market value of final goods within domestic territory. GNP = GDP + NFIA. NNP = GNP - Depreciation. National Income = NNP at Factor Cost = NNP at Market Price - Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
Explain the difference between Nominal GDP and Real GDP.

Proof: Nominal GDP = GDP at current prices. Real GDP = GDP at constant prices (base year prices). Real GDP = Nominal GDP / Price Index × 100. Real GDP is a better measure of economic growth as it removes price changes.
Explain the concept of Value Added.
Proof: Value Added = Output - Intermediate Consumption. It is the contribution of a firm to GDP. Sum of value added by all firms = GDP. It avoids double counting.
Explain the difference between Factor Cost and Market Price.
Proof: Factor Cost = cost of factors of production (rent, wages, interest, profit). Market Price = Factor Cost + Indirect Taxes - Subsidies. GDP at MP = GDP at FC + Indirect Taxes - Subsidies.
Explain the concept of NFIA.
Proof: NFIA = Factor Income from Abroad - Factor Income to Abroad. GNP = GDP + NFIA. If NFIA is positive, GNP > GDP. If negative, GNP < GDP.

formulas: Money: medium of exchange, measure of value, store of value
Functions of Money: Primary (medium of exchange, measure of value), Secondary (store of value, standard of deferred payment, transfer of value)
Money Supply (M1) = Currency with Public + Demand Deposits + Other Deposits with RBI
M2 = M1 + Savings Deposits with Post Office
M3 = M1 + Time Deposits with Banks
M4 = M3 + Total Deposits with Post Office
High Powered Money (H) = Currency with Public + Cash Reserves with RBI
Money Multiplier = Money Supply / High Powered Money
Credit Creation = Initial Deposit × (1/CRR)
CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio): % of deposits kept with RBI
SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio): % of deposits kept as liquid assets
Repo Rate: rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks
Reverse Repo Rate: rate at which RBI borrows from commercial banks
Bank Rate: rate at which RBI lends long-term
Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): emergency borrowing by banks
Open Market Operations (OMO): buying/selling of government securities
Quantitative Tools: CRR, SLR, Repo, Reverse Repo, Bank Rate, OMO
Qualitative Tools: Margin Requirement, Moral Suasion, Selective Credit Control
derivations: Explain the functions of money.

Proof: Primary Functions: (1) Medium of Exchange: money acts as intermediary in exchange. (2) Measure of Value: money measures value of goods and services. Secondary Functions: (3) Store of Value: money can be saved for future. (4) Standard of Deferred Payment: money used for future payments. (5) Transfer of Value: money helps in transferring purchasing power.
Explain the concept of Money Multiplier.

Proof: Money Multiplier = Money Supply / High Powered Money. It shows how much money supply increases with increase in high powered money. Money Multiplier = 1/CRR (if no excess reserves). Example: CRR = 10%, Money Multiplier = 1/0.10 = 10. Initial deposit of ₹1,000 creates total deposits of ₹10,000.
Explain the process of Credit Creation by Commercial Banks.

Proof: Banks create credit by lending out deposits. Initial deposit = ₹1,000. CRR = 10%. Bank keeps ₹100, lends ₹900. Borrower deposits ₹900 in another bank. That bank keeps ₹90, lends ₹810. Process continues. Total credit = 1,000 × (1/0.10) = ₹10,000. Credit Creation = Initial Deposit × (1/CRR).
Explain the instruments of Monetary Policy.

Proof: Quantitative Tools: (1) CRR: % of deposits kept with RBI. (2) SLR: % of deposits kept as liquid assets. (3) Repo Rate: rate at which RBI lends to banks. (4) Reverse Repo: rate at which RBI borrows. (5) Bank Rate: long-term lending rate. (6) OMO: buying/selling of securities. Qualitative Tools: Margin Requirement, Moral Suasion, Selective Credit Control.
Explain the difference between CRR and SLR.

Proof: CRR is kept with RBI in cash. SLR is kept with the bank itself in liquid assets (gold, government securities). Both are percentages of deposits. CRR is maintained for monetary control, SLR for liquidity and solvency.
Explain the difference between Repo Rate and Reverse Repo Rate.

Proof: Repo Rate: rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks (short-term). Reverse Repo Rate: rate at which RBI borrows from commercial banks. Repo Rate > Reverse Repo Rate. Both are used for monetary control.
Explain the concept of High Powered Money.
Proof: High Powered Money (H) = Currency with Public + Cash Reserves with RBI. It is the base money created by RBI. Money Supply = Money Multiplier × High Powered Money.

formulas: Aggregate Demand (AD) = C + I + G + (X - M)
Aggregate Supply (AS) = Y = C + S
Consumption Function: C = a + bY
a = autonomous consumption, b = MPC
MPC (Marginal Propensity to Consume) = ΔC/ΔY
MPS (Marginal Propensity to Save) = ΔS/ΔY
MPC + MPS = 1
APC (Average Propensity to Consume) = C/Y
APS (Average Propensity to Save) = S/Y
APC + APS = 1
Saving Function: S = -a + (1-b)Y
Investment Multiplier (k) = 1/(1-MPC) = 1/MPS
ΔY = k × ΔI
Equilibrium: AD = AS, or S = I
Excess Demand: AD > AS at full employment
Deficient Demand: AD < AS at full employment
Full Employment: all willing workers get jobs
Inflationary Gap: excess demand leading to inflation
Deflationary Gap: deficient demand leading to deflation
derivations: Explain the concept of Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply.
Proof: AD = C + I + G + (X - M). AS = Y = C + S. Equilibrium occurs when AD = AS. At equilibrium, planned spending equals planned output. If AD > AS, excess demand. If AD < AS, deficient demand.
Explain the Consumption Function.

Proof: C = a + bY. a = autonomous consumption (minimum consumption at zero income). b = MPC = ΔC/ΔY. Consumption increases with income but less than proportionately. APC = C/Y. APC decreases as income increases.
Explain the Saving Function.
Proof: S = -a + (1-b)Y. -a = dissaving at zero income. (1-b) = MPS = ΔS/ΔY. Saving increases with income. MPS + MPC = 1. APS + APC = 1.
Explain the Investment Multiplier.

Proof: k = 1/(1-MPC) = 1/MPS. ΔY = k × ΔI. Example: MPC = 0.8, k = 1/0.2 = 5. If investment increases by ₹100, income increases by ₹500. Multiplier works because one person's spending becomes another's income.
Explain the concept of Excess Demand and Deficient Demand.

Proof: Excess Demand: AD > AS at full employment. Leads to inflation. Inflationary Gap = Excess Demand. Deficient Demand: AD < AS at full employment. Leads to deflation and unemployment. Deflationary Gap = Deficient Demand. Both are corrected by fiscal and monetary policies.
Explain the concept of Full Employment.

Proof: Full employment: all willing and able workers get jobs at prevailing wage rate. It does not mean zero unemployment. Some frictional and structural unemployment may exist. At full employment, AD = AS.
Explain the difference between MPC and MPS.
Proof: MPC = ΔC/ΔY, MPS = ΔS/ΔY. MPC + MPS = 1. MPC is between 0 and 1. MPS is between 0 and 1. Higher MPC means higher consumption, lower saving. Higher MPS means higher saving, lower consumption.

(4) Consumption Function: C = a + bY. (5) Saving Function: S = -a + (1-b)Y. (6) MPC + MPS = 1, APC + APS = 1. (7) Investment Multiplier k = 1/(1-MPC) = 1/MPS. (8) ΔY = k × ΔI. (9) Excess Demand: AD > AS. (10) Deficient Demand: AD < AS.

formulas: Government Budget: annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditures
Objectives: Reallocation of resources, Redistribution of income, Economic stability, Economic growth, Employment generation
Components: Revenue Budget and Capital Budget
Revenue Receipts: Tax Revenue + Non-Tax Revenue
Tax Revenue: Direct Taxes + Indirect Taxes
Direct Taxes: Income Tax, Corporate Tax
Indirect Taxes: GST, Customs, Excise
Non-Tax Revenue: Interest, Dividends, Fees, Fines
Capital Receipts: Borrowings, Recovery of Loans, Disinvestment
Revenue Expenditure: expenditure that does not create assets
Capital Expenditure: expenditure that creates assets or reduces liabilities
Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure - Revenue Receipts
Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - Total Receipts (excluding borrowings)
Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payments
Budget Deficit = Total Expenditure - Total Receipts
Balanced Budget: Receipts = Expenditure
Surplus Budget: Receipts > Expenditure
Deficit Budget: Receipts < Expenditure
Crowding Out Effect: government borrowing reduces private investment
Public Debt: Internal + External
derivations: Explain the components of Government Budget.

Proof: Government Budget has two components: (1) Revenue Budget: Revenue Receipts (Tax + Non-Tax) and Revenue Expenditure. (2) Capital Budget: Capital Receipts (Borrowings, Recovery of Loans, Disinvestment) and Capital Expenditure. Revenue Receipts do not create liabilities, Capital Receipts do.
Explain the concept of Revenue Deficit.

Proof: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure - Revenue Receipts. It shows excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts. It indicates that government is spending more than it earns from revenue sources. It is financed by borrowings.
Explain the concept of Fiscal Deficit.

Proof: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - Total Receipts (excluding borrowings). It shows total borrowing requirement of the government. It includes Revenue Deficit + Capital Expenditure - Non-Debt Capital Receipts. It is an indicator of government's indebtedness.
Explain the concept of Primary Deficit.

Proof: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payments. It shows Fiscal Deficit excluding interest payments on past debt. It indicates current fiscal position of the government. If Primary Deficit is zero, Fiscal Deficit is due to past debt only.
Explain the objectives of Government Budget.

Proof: Objectives: (1) Reallocation of resources: government allocates resources to priority sectors. (2) Redistribution of income: through taxes and subsidies. (3) Economic stability: to control inflation and deflation. (4) Economic growth: to promote growth. (5) Employment generation: to create jobs. (6) Reducing regional disparities.
Explain the difference between Revenue Receipts and Capital Receipts.

Proof: Revenue Receipts: do not create liabilities or reduce assets. Examples: Tax Revenue, Non-Tax Revenue. Capital Receipts: create liabilities or reduce assets. Examples: Borrowings, Recovery of Loans, Disinvestment. Revenue Receipts are recurring, Capital Receipts are non-recurring.
Explain the difference between Revenue Expenditure and Capital Expenditure.

Proof: Revenue Expenditure: does not create assets or reduce liabilities. Examples: Salaries, Interest Payments, Subsidies. Capital Expenditure: creates assets or reduces liabilities. Examples: Construction of roads, Repayment of loans. Revenue Expenditure is recurring, Capital Expenditure is non-recurring.

formulas: Balance of Payments (BoP): record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and rest of the world
Components: Current Account and Capital Account
Current Account: visible trade (goods), invisible trade (services), unilateral transfers
Capital Account: foreign investment, loans, banking capital, other capital
Balance of Trade = Exports - Imports
Current Account Balance = Balance of Trade + Net Invisible + Net Transfers
Capital Account Balance = Inflows - Outflows
BoP Always Balances: Current Account + Capital Account = 0
If Current Account Deficit, Capital Account Surplus
If Current Account Surplus, Capital Account Deficit
Foreign Exchange Rate: price of one currency in terms of another
Fixed Exchange Rate: pegged by government
Flexible Exchange Rate: determined by market forces
Managed Float: market forces with government intervention
Depreciation: fall in value of domestic currency
Appreciation: rise in value of domestic currency
Devaluation: official reduction in value of currency
Revaluation: official increase in value of currency
Demand for Foreign Exchange: for imports, tourism, investment
Supply of Foreign Exchange: from exports, tourism, investment
derivations: Explain the components of Balance of Payments.

Proof: BoP has two components: (1) Current Account: visible trade (goods), invisible trade (services), unilateral transfers. (2) Capital Account: foreign investment, loans, banking capital, other capital. BoP always balances: Current Account + Capital Account = 0.
Explain the concept of Balance of Trade.
Proof: Balance of Trade = Exports - Imports. If Exports > Imports, Trade Surplus. If Exports < Imports, Trade Deficit. It is a part of Current Account. It includes only visible goods, not services.
Explain the difference between Current Account and Capital Account.

Proof: Current Account: records trade in goods, services, and unilateral transfers. Capital Account: records foreign investment, loans, banking capital. Current Account affects current income, Capital Account affects assets and liabilities. Current Account + Capital Account = 0.
Explain the concept of Foreign Exchange Rate.

Proof: Foreign Exchange Rate: price of one currency in terms of another. Types: (1) Fixed: pegged by government. (2) Flexible: determined by market forces. (3) Managed Float: market forces with government intervention. Demand for forex comes from imports, supply from exports.
Explain the difference between Depreciation and Devaluation.

Proof: Depreciation: fall in value of domestic currency in a flexible exchange rate system (market forces). Devaluation: official reduction in value of domestic currency in a fixed exchange rate system (government decision). Both make exports cheaper and imports costlier.
Explain the difference between Appreciation and Revaluation.

Proof: Appreciation: rise in value of domestic currency in a flexible exchange rate system (market forces). Revaluation: official increase in value of domestic currency in a fixed exchange rate system (government decision). Both make exports costlier and imports cheaper.
Explain the concept of Current Account Deficit.

Proof: Current Account Deficit = Current Account Receipts < Current Account Payments. It means country is spending more on imports and transfers than it earns from exports and transfers. It is financed by Capital Account Surplus (borrowings, investments).

formulas: Indian Economy on Eve of Independence: agricultural economy, low GDP, high poverty
Five Year Plans: started 1951, aimed at economic development
Objectives of Plans: Growth, Equity, Self-reliance, Modernisation
Green Revolution: increased food production (1960s-70s)
White Revolution: increased milk production (Operation Flood)
Industrial Policy Resolution 1956: emphasised public sector
Licensing Policy: industrial licensing for private sector
Small Scale Industries: promoted for employment
Foreign Trade: import substitution, export promotion
Economic Reforms 1991: LPG (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation)
Liberalisation: removal of unnecessary controls
Privatisation: transfer of ownership to private sector
Globalisation: integration with world economy
New Industrial Policy 1991: reduced licensing, allowed foreign investment
Disinvestment: sale of government equity in PSUs
NAFTA, WTO: international trade agreements
Balance of Payments Crisis 1991: forex reserves depleted
IMF Loan: conditionalities for reforms
derivations: Explain the state of Indian Economy on the eve of Independence.

Proof: (1) Agricultural economy: 85% population depended on agriculture. (2) Low GDP: stagnant economy. (3) High poverty: low standard of living. (4) Low life expectancy: 32 years. (5) High illiteracy: 16% literacy. (6) Low industrialisation: few industries. (7) Foreign trade: export of raw materials, import of finished goods. (8) Infrastructure: underdeveloped.
Explain the objectives of Five Year Plans.

Proof: Objectives: (1) Growth: increase in GDP and per capita income. (2) Equity: reduce inequality. (3) Self-reliance: reduce dependence on foreign aid. (4) Modernisation: adopt new technology. (5) Employment: create jobs. (6) Poverty reduction. (7) Food security.
Explain the Green Revolution.

Proof: Green Revolution: increase in food production through use of HYV seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation. Started in 1960s. Increased wheat and rice production. Made India self-sufficient in food. Critics: increased regional disparities, environmental damage.
Explain the Economic Reforms of 1991.

Proof: Reforms: LPG (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation). Liberalisation: removal of licensing, reduced government control. Privatisation: disinvestment, transfer of ownership. Globalisation: integration with world economy, foreign trade, investment. Reasons: BoP crisis, high fiscal deficit, inflation.
Explain the New Industrial Policy 1991.

Proof: Features: (1) Reduced industrial licensing. (2) Allowed foreign investment. (3) Disinvestment of PSUs. (4) Reduced public sector monopoly. (5) Encouraged private sector. (6) Increased competition. (7) Technology upgradation.
Explain the impact of Economic Reforms.

Proof: Positive: (1) Higher GDP growth. (2) Increased foreign investment. (3) Better technology. (4) Increased exports. (5) Rise of service sector. Negative: (1) Increased inequality. (2) Jobless growth. (3) Decline of small industries. (4) Environmental degradation. (5) Regional disparities.
Explain the difference between Green Revolution and White Revolution.

Proof: Green Revolution: increased food production (wheat, rice). White Revolution: increased milk production (Operation Flood). Green Revolution: use of HYV seeds, fertilisers. White Revolution: cooperative movement, dairy development.

formulas: Poverty: inability to meet basic needs
Poverty Line: minimum income/consumption level
Head Count Ratio: % of population below poverty line
Poverty Gap: difference between poverty line and actual income

Causes of Poverty: Unemployment, Inflation, Inequality, Population
Human Capital: knowledge, skills, health of people
Human Capital Formation: investment in education, health, training
Sources: Education, Health, On-the-job training, Migration, Information
Rural Development: improvement in rural areas
Rural Credit: institutional and non-institutional sources
Agricultural Marketing: process of selling agricultural produce
Employment: types: Self-employment, Wage employment, Casual, Regular
Unemployment: types: Frictional, Structural, Cyclical, Seasonal, Disguised
Unemployment Rate = Unemployed / Labour Force × 100
Labour Force Participation Rate = Labour Force / Population × 100
Inflation: rise in general price level
Types: Demand-pull, Cost-push
Causes: Increase in money supply, increase in demand, increase in cost
Measures: Monetary policy, Fiscal policy
derivations: Explain the concept of Poverty.

Proof: Poverty: inability to meet basic needs (food, clothing, shelter). Types: (1) Absolute Poverty: income below poverty line. (2) Relative Poverty: income less than others. Causes: Unemployment, Inflation, Inequality, Population growth. Measures: Poverty alleviation programs.
Explain Human Capital Formation.

Proof: Human Capital Formation: investment in education, health, training. Sources: (1) Education. (2) Health. (3) On-the-job training. (4) Migration. (5) Information. Importance: increases productivity, income, economic growth. Difference from Human Development: Human Development is broader (includes freedom, equality).
Explain Rural Development.

Proof: Rural Development: improvement in rural areas. Components: (1) Rural Credit: institutional (banks, cooperatives) and non-institutional (moneylenders). (2) Agricultural Marketing: process of selling produce. (3) Rural Employment: schemes like MGNREGA. (4) Rural Infrastructure: roads, electricity, water. (5) Rural Education and Health.
Explain the types of Unemployment.

Proof: Types: (1) Frictional: temporary, between jobs. (2) Structural: due to change in structure of economy. (3) Cyclical: due to business cycle. (4) Seasonal: due to seasonal nature of work. (5) Disguised: more people working than needed. (6) Open: willing to work but no job.
Explain the concept of Inflation.

Proof: Inflation: rise in general price level. Types: (1) Demand-pull: increase in demand. (2) Cost-push: increase in cost. Causes: Increase in money supply, increase in demand, increase in cost. Measures: Monetary policy (CRR, SLR, Repo), Fiscal policy (taxes, expenditure).
Explain the difference between Human Capital and Human Development.

Proof: Human Capital: investment in education, health, training for productivity. Human Development: broader concept, includes freedom, equality, health, education. Human Capital is a means to economic growth, Human Development is an end in itself.
Explain the difference between Poverty and Unemployment.

Proof: Poverty: inability to meet basic needs. Unemployment: willing to work but no job. Poverty can be caused by unemployment. Both are challenges facing Indian economy. Both require government intervention.

Explain Pakistan's Economic Reforms.

formulas: Management: process of getting things done through others
Characteristics: Goal-oriented, All-pervasive, Multidimensional, Continuous, Intangible, Composite, Dynamic
Objectives: Organisational, Social, Personal
Importance: Achieves goals, Increases efficiency, Creates dynamic organisation, Helps in development, Improves standard of living
Nature: Art, Science, Profession
Management as Art: practical knowledge, personal skill, creativity
Management as Science: systematic body of knowledge, principles, cause-effect
Management as Profession: specialised knowledge, code of conduct, service motive
Levels of Management: Top, Middle, Operational
Top Level: CEO, Board of Directors; functions: policy making, strategy
Middle Level: Departmental heads; functions: implement policies, coordinate
Operational Level: Supervisors; functions: supervise workers, daily operations
Functions of Management: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Controlling
Coordination: integration of all activities
Coordination is the essence of management
derivations: Explain the characteristics of Management.

Proof: (1) Goal-oriented: management aims to achieve goals. (2) All-pervasive: applicable to all organisations. (3) Multidimensional: manages work, people, operations. (4) Continuous: never-ending process. (5) Intangible: cannot be seen but felt. (6) Composite: combination of art, science, profession. (7) Dynamic: adapts to changes.
Explain the objectives of Management.

Proof: (1) Organisational: profit, growth, survival. (2) Social: provide employment, protect environment, community service. (3) Personal: employee satisfaction, salary, growth. All three are interrelated.
Explain the importance of Management.

Proof: (1) Achieves goals: coordinates resources. (2) Increases efficiency: reduces cost, increases productivity. (3) Creates dynamic organisation: adapts to changes. (4) Helps in development: of society and nation. (5) Improves standard of living: quality goods and services.
Explain Management as Art, Science, and Profession.

Proof: Art: practical knowledge, personal skill, creativity. Science: systematic knowledge, principles, cause-effect. Profession: specialised knowledge, code of conduct, service motive. Management is a combination of all three.
Explain the levels of Management.

Proof: (1) Top Level: CEO, Board; functions: policy making, strategy, coordination. (2) Middle Level: Departmental heads; functions: implement policies, coordinate, motivate. (3) Operational Level: Supervisors; functions: supervise workers, daily operations, report.
Explain the functions of Management.

Proof: (1) Planning: deciding in advance. (2) Organising: arranging resources. (3) Staffing: recruitment, selection, training. (4) Directing: leading, motivating, communicating. (5) Controlling: monitoring, correcting. Coordination integrates all functions.
Explain Coordination as the essence of Management.

Proof: Coordination: integration of all activities and efforts. It is the essence of management because: (1) Integrates all functions. (2) Ensures unity of action. (3) Avoids duplication. (4) Achieves goals efficiently. (5) Present at all levels.

formulas: Principles of Management: general guidelines for managerial action
Taylor's Scientific Management: science-based approach

Taylor's Techniques: Functional Foremanship, Standardisation, Simplification, Method Study, Motion Study, Time Study, Fatigue Study, Differential Piece Wage
Fayol's Administrative Management: 14 principles

Fayol's 14 Principles: Division of Work, Authority and Responsibility, Discipline, Unity of Command, Unity of Direction, Subordination of Individual Interest, Remuneration, Centralisation, Scalar Chain, Order, Equity, Stability of Tenure, Initiative, Esprit de Corps
Unity of Command: one boss for one employee
Unity of Direction: one head, one plan for one group
Scalar Chain: line of authority from top to bottom
Gang Plank: direct communication between same level employees
Esprit de Corps: team spirit
Difference: Taylor focused on shop floor, Fayol on entire organisation
derivations: Explain Taylor's Scientific Management.

Proof: Taylor's Scientific Management: science-based approach to management. Principles: (1) Science, not rule of thumb. (2) Harmony, not discord. (3) Cooperation, not individualism. (4) Development of each person. Techniques: Functional Foremanship, Standardisation, Simplification, Method Study, Motion Study, Time Study, Fatigue Study, Differential Piece Wage.
Explain Fayol's 14 Principles of Management.

Proof: (1) Division of Work: specialisation. (2) Authority and Responsibility: balance. (3) Discipline: obedience. (4) Unity of Command: one boss. (5) Unity of Direction: one plan. (6) Subordination of Individual Interest: organisation first. (7) Remuneration: fair pay. (8) Centralisation: balance. (9) Scalar Chain: line of authority. (10) Order: right place. (11) Equity: fairness. (12) Stability of Tenure: job security. (13) Initiative: encourage ideas. (14) Esprit de Corps: team spirit.
Explain the difference between Taylor and Fayol.

Proof: Taylor: focused on shop floor, scientific management, techniques. Fayol: focused on entire organisation, administrative management, principles. Taylor: bottom-up approach. Fayol: top-down approach. Both contributed to management thought.
Explain Unity of Command and Unity of Direction.
Proof: Unity of Command: one employee should have only one boss. Unity of Direction: one head and one plan for a group of activities with same objective. Both avoid confusion and duplication.
Explain Scalar Chain and Gang Plank.

Proof: Scalar Chain: line of authority from top to bottom. Gang Plank: direct communication between employees of same level without following scalar chain. It is used in emergencies to speed up communication.
Explain the techniques of Scientific Management.

Proof: (1) Functional Foremanship: separation of planning and execution. (2) Standardisation: setting standards. (3) Simplification: eliminating unnecessary products. (4) Method Study: finding best method. (5) Motion Study: eliminating unnecessary motions. (6) Time Study: setting time standards. (7) Fatigue Study: reducing fatigue. (8) Differential Piece Wage: higher wages for higher output.
Explain the importance of Principles of Management.
Proof: (1) Provide guidelines. (2) Increase efficiency. (3) Aid in decision making. (4) Help in coordination. (5) Meet changing environment. (6) Social responsibility. (7) Training and development.

Procedure: steps to carry out activities
